images.caption: Lapworth Junction,, Stratford-on-Avon Canal As a narrowboat emerges from Lock 20 on the right to proceed towards the camera and beyond to the Grand Union Canal, the "bridge-testing party" of historians seen in an earlier picture have moved on to another cantilevered split bridge, though here there seems to be less room on the bridge for all their number.  The bridge they are standing on was a former stop-lock -- a gate recess can be seen in the wall on the right-hand side -- between the Stratford-on-Avon and Grand Union Canals that had been blocked during a dispute between the two canal companies about water rights.  Thereafter boats from the Grand Union Canal wishing to go to Stratford had to pass up Lock 20 to the right, turn through 180 degrees and immediately pass down through another lock.  More recently British Waterways, now owner of both canals has re-opened the old direct and level passage.

images.filename: Hotel boat and butty, Stratford-upon-Avon Canal near Solihull - geograph.org.uk - 1717406.jpg
images.caption:
Hotel boat and butty, Stratford-upon-Avon Canal near Solihull There are many pairs of boats operated as Hotels. The powered boat pulls an unpowered "butty".
By the towpath is the butty ( "Karna Taka"), a narrowboat with no method of propulsion and a large wooden tiller and rudder for steering. This one has guest accommodation (four bunks + lounge) and crew accommodation. Moored alongside is the motorised narrowboat (including galley, crew quarters, and maybe four bunks for guests). This boat will tow the butty. It is probably narrowboat "Rose".
Both these boats are as long as they can be (71 feet) to fit in the narrow locks on most canals, or as a pair in wide locks.

This pair of boats was climbing the Lapworth flight of locks in front of us, and we expected slow progress, but no! Their crew and guests were very slick despite the wet conditions!
